name: Gibbus deformity

lead: A gibbus is a sharply angled bend in the spine, usually in the chest or upper-lower back, where one or a few vertebrae have collapsed at the front and the rest of the column bends around that point. From behind it shows as a localized bony bump rather than a smooth, rounded hunch.

In looks discussions it is mentioned mainly to separate it from postural kyphosis (slouching, 'hump' posture), which is a soft, flexible curve that can change with training. Knowing which one you have determines whether posture work, such as strengthening and mobility, can improve the upper-back silhouette at all.

paras: Posture-focused routines (back and shoulder strengthening, stretching, ergonomic changes) are aimed at the flexible, postural type of rounding. A gibbus is structural: the shape comes from the vertebrae themselves, so it is evaluated by clinicians, typically with imaging, and managed according to its cause.

The causes include spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease), certain inherited metabolic disorders such as mucopolysaccharidosis type I, congenital vertebral malformations and fractures. Some of these can compress the spinal cord or affect breathing, so a sudden or progressive angular bump with pain or neurological symptoms is a medical matter. Treatment depends on the cause and can include drug therapy, bracing in growing children, or surgery.

angle.text: Knowing the difference between a gibbus and postural hump lets someone direct posture work at the type of rounding it can change. A gibbus is assessed medically, and treatment of the underlying cause is what can change the contour.

lead: A gibbus deformity is an abrupt, angular kyphosis of the spine: instead of a smooth outward curve, the back bends sharply at one point, producing a visible bony prominence. Medical sources classify it as a structural kyphosis, meaning the vertebral bones themselves are affected, in contrast to postural kyphosis, which is associated with slouching and has normal-appearing vertebrae [1].

For people interested in improving their appearance, the relevance is differential. Rounded upper-back posture ('hump') is a common concern, and postural kyphosis in young people is described as reversible by correcting muscle imbalances [1]. A gibbus does not behave that way, so telling the two apart determines whether posture training is a sensible route to a straighter-looking back.

The classic cause is spinal tuberculosis, where infection destroys the front of the vertebral bodies and the column collapses into a sharp curve [2][3]. It is also a recognized feature of some inherited conditions, notably Hurler disease (mucopolysaccharidosis type I), in which infants can develop a spinal gibbus [4].

paras: Kyphosis is an exaggerated forward curve of the upper spine. The most common form is postural, linked to slouching, with normal-looking vertebrae and discs; in young people it is described as reversible with correction of muscle imbalances [1]. Structural kyphosis involves the bones, and gibbus is the sharply angled variant, often described as a sequel to tuberculosis [1].

Because a gibbus concentrates the bend into one or a few segments, it looks like a pointed prominence in the midline of the back rather than a gradual rounding. A 1987 orthopedic paper described methods for predicting the final gibbus angle in tuberculosis of the spine, reflecting how clinicians track the deformity over time [5].

In spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease), infection usually spreads through the blood to the thoracic and upper lumbar spine, destroys the anterior vertebral body and produces collapse with a sharp angular curve; in children the curve can worsen during growth spurts [2]. Reviews describe destruction of the disc space and adjacent vertebrae, anterior wedging, kyphosis and gibbus formation [4].

In mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler disease), accumulation of glycosaminoglycans affects bone, and affected infants develop a spinal gibbus alongside other skeletal and systemic features [6]. Other kyphosis causes in the general literature include congenital malformed or fused vertebrae and, in older people, compression fractures [1].

Postural kyphosis is smooth and flexible and is addressed with posture retraining and strengthening exercises; structural kyphosis is described as harder to manage, and posture correction alone may not change it [1]. Clinicians generally use examination and imaging to tell them apart.

Management follows the cause. For spinal tuberculosis, multidrug chemotherapy is the cornerstone and can be curative with minimal residual kyphosis; surgery (debridement, deformity correction and fusion) is reserved for neurological deficit or severe kyphosis [3]. Standard antibiotic courses run for several months [2]. For growing children with structural kyphosis, bracing may be used, and surgery may be recommended for severe cases [1].

Published literature consists mainly of reviews and case series on the underlying conditions rather than on appearance outcomes. Reviews of spinal tuberculosis describe presentation, imaging and treatment, including kyphotic deformity [3][4]; reviews of mucopolysaccharidosis describe the gibbus as a typical skeletal sign [6]. A 1987 study examined predicting the gibbus angle in spinal tuberculosis [5]. No studies were found testing posture exercises as a treatment for gibbus specifically.

timeline.event: British surgeon Percivall Pott describes tuberculosis of the spine, later named Pott disease [2].
A paper on predicting the angle of gibbus deformity in spinal tuberculosis is published in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery [5].
